The data behind the model is still a product problem.

I'm a Product Data Operations Program Manager (AI Search) at Meta, where I own the data operations behind AI search, ranking, and recommendation — 15+ ML annotation programs, a 135-person global org, and the quality bar that Llama-based classifiers and LLM-as-judge systems get trained and evaluated against.

Before Meta, I led product at Google (MBA capstone, autonomous dispatch), interned on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and spent five years at Maruti Suzuki taking connected-vehicle and IoT products — including a 5,000-responder emergency SOS system — from zero to launch.

I hold an MBA (STEM) in Product Management & Strategy from the University of Wisconsin–Madison and a B.Tech from Delhi College of Engineering. Along the way, a root-cause fix I led on a vehicle noise issue earned a patent and $2.6M in royalties.

A few programs worth zooming in on.

search & ranking

Social RAG Query Intent Classifier

Defined the labeling taxonomy and iterated guidelines through model error analysis for Facebook's query-intent classifier on Llama 3.3 (70B). The taxonomy had to hold up across ambiguous, multi-intent queries — the kind that break most rule-based routing.

95.8% precision · 97.9% recall
why it mattered

Search on a feed built around people, not documents, breaks the moment intent gets flattened to keywords — "gift for someone who just got promoted" has to route differently than "promo codes." The classifier runs on Llama 3.3 70B, the model Meta shipped at a fraction of the compute cost of its 405B sibling specifically so reasoning like this could run in production at social-platform scale. Getting the taxonomy right was the difference between search that reads what a query means and search that just reads its words.

eval design

LLM-as-Judge Alignment Study

Built a 700-sample stratified eval, taxonomized failures into binary pass/fail rubrics, and refined judge prompts through false-positive/false-negative analysis. Most of the gain came from finding where the judge and human raters disagreed for structural reasons, not just noisy labels.

92.4% human–AI alignment
why it mattered

LLM-as-a-judge exists because human review can't scale to millions of model outputs — but a judge with a loose rubric just launders human bias into a different, less visible bias. Judges are known to favor longer answers or waver on ambiguous edge cases, which is exactly what the FP/FN analysis targeted, tightening the rubric until the judge's calls converged with human raters far more often. At 92.4% alignment, this became a judge Meta could actually trust to grade at a scale no review team could match.

data quality

Annotation Quality Overhaul

Root-caused a search-relevance regression to training-data quality drift, then rebuilt the quality methodology behind Meta's annotation pipeline from the ground up — instrumentation, reviewer calibration, and the taxonomy itself.

66% → 98% label accuracy
why it mattered

Andrew Ng's data-centric AI argument is that most real-world model gains come from the data, not the architecture — most teams just don't act like they believe it. This program was the practical test of that idea inside Meta: same models, same infrastructure, and a 32-point swing in label accuracy from rebuilding instrumentation, reviewer calibration, and the taxonomy underneath. The payoff showed up downstream, in Facebook's 10% search relevance gain and a chunk of the 27% DAP growth — proof the fix was upstream of the model the whole time.

commerce

Bridgerton × Marketplace

Partnered with product and marketing to launch Netflix's themed commerce activation on Facebook Marketplace end to end — from concept through giveaways and merchandising.

+25% Marketplace engagement
why it mattered

Bridgerton isn't a niche show to court — its most recent season premiere landed at #1 on Netflix's Global Top 10 with tens of millions of views in its opening week, and Netflix now runs dozens of brand collaborations around every release. Marketplace's job was to be the partner selling an experience rather than merchandise — Regency-styled furniture, fashion, and tea-time pieces timed to launch week, when fan intent to buy into the world peaks. Running that with the same roadmap-partners-execution rigor as a core product launch is what separated it from a one-off marketing stunt.

IoT · automotive

Suzuki V2X Emergency SOS

Led GTM and a 5-member cross-functional team to launch an Azure IoT-based SOS product for connected vehicles, from architecture decisions through responder onboarding.

−30 min ambulance response · 5,000+ responders
why it mattered

Automated crash-and-SOS systems exist because regulators found they work: similar eCall-style systems are estimated to cut emergency response times by up to half and save roughly 2,500 lives a year in the EU alone, simply because a car can raise the alarm when nobody inside can. For cardiac arrest specifically, survival odds drop 7–10% for every minute without treatment — which is exactly the kind of window a 30-minute average improvement moves. It's now part of the emergency-response workflow for 5,000+ responders, which means those 30 minutes show up as outcomes, not just a number on a dashboard.

connected vehicle

Suzuki Connect

A real-time vehicle monitoring SaaS shaped by 200+ customer interviews — positioning and pricing were rebuilt around what actually moved theft-recovery and renewal decisions.

−10% theft complaints · +12% YoY subs
why it mattered

Connected-vehicle telematics has become a real security category, not a nice-to-have — the stolen-vehicle-recovery market alone runs into the tens of billions of dollars and keeps growing at a double-digit clip, partly because insurers now discount premiums for cars that carry it. Suzuki Connect's pricing and positioning were rebuilt around 200+ customer interviews instead of the original roadmap, and following what customers actually said moved their renewal decision — not just theft-recovery messaging — is what took it from a feature to a subscription people kept paying for.
